name: Yusuf Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, I'm 58, and I've been head of livestock, well, the only livestock man, on the Ashcombe estate for twenty-three years. Me and Maureen live in the tied cottage by the grain store, which means the house comes with the job. She does mornings in the primary school kitchen. Our daughter Aisha is a nurse in the city and our son Liam drives lorries.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five to check the suckler cows, 180 of them, and the 300 ewes up on Long Hill. Pete does most of the arable, the wheat and barley, and I help him at harvest on the old John Deere. I like calving, honestly, getting a big calf out alive at three in the morning still makes my week. What wears me out is the land agent, Mr Cole, emailing Pete about cutting costs, and my knees on the cattle grids in winter. They sold the dairy herd two years ago and Davey's job went with it, so you never quite relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Right. Well, I don't use any of it, so I'm half hoping it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union branch I'd say good, now let's get back to what matters, which is wages and housing for farm workers. In the pub I'd say I told you so. I don't go online, Maureen does the Facebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix my real problem. I'm on low pay, we've got about three weeks of money in the bank, and if Mr Cole decides the cattle don't pay, I lose the job and the roof in one go. AI being hype doesn't change that one bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, calving in March, lambing in April. I'd ask the union rep, Shirin, again about what rights I've got on the cottage when I retire. And I'd try to put fifty pounds a month away, which we've said every year and never managed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, if I'm honest. It's a relief that nothing big comes, but the small worries don't go anywhere. I still lie awake about the cottage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cottage keeps you up. What happens to it when you retire?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I stop working, I have to give the cottage back. So retirement is the day we become homeless, unless something changes. That's the deal with a tied house. We've put our names down on the council list, but they told Maureen it's years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the estate cut the cattle, what would you do the next morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Shirin first, then I'd ring Aisha. There's only two other big farms within twenty miles and they've both got their own men. I'm not proud, I'd take anything, but there's nothing round here to take.

say: I'd tell the **union branch** that farm workers' pay and housing matter more than any AI story.
I'd say **I told you so** in the pub, because I never trusted the hype.
think: My real fear is losing the **job and the cottage** together, because the house comes with the work.
Hype or not, **three weeks of savings** means one bad decision by the estate sinks us.
do: Keep **calving and lambing** on the usual dates and give the estate no reason to cut the cattle.
Ask the union rep about **cottage rights** at retirement before spring.
Try to save **fifty pounds a month**, though we've never managed it before.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing big happens, but still **tired** from the old worries.
S0.quote: When I stop working, I have to give the cottage back. So retirement is the day we become homeless, unless something changes.
fieldNote: His biggest pressure has nothing to do with **AI**: a tied cottage that goes when the job goes.
Even with no change, he talks about the estate's **cost-cutting** as a live threat after the dairy herd went.
He leans on the **union** first and family second, and never mentions doing anything online.

steps.text: Keep the March calving and April lambing on the usual dates
Ask the union rep about tied-cottage rights at retirement
Put fifty pounds a month into the post office account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking tasks. That's the office, then, not me. Robots slower. Slower than what, though?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at the branch that the estate office will use this to cut Mr Cole's paperwork, and they'll pocket the saving, not us. I'd want the union pushing for a law that says if machines save money, workers get a share. That's what I'd say, loudly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the cows still need a man for a few years. But Mr Cole already plans everything on a spreadsheet, and if a computer tells him the herd loses money, he'll believe the computer over me. I'm the one who knows which cow calves badly, and that won't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well. I'd go to every union meeting about this and sign whatever petition comes. I won't learn the computer stuff, I'm too old and I don't trust it. I'd ask Liam to help Maureen and me put a bit by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then a bit angry. It's the same story as the dairy herd. Somebody far away decides on a screen, and somebody here packs his van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer could tell Mr Cole the herd loses money. Has something like that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly how the dairy went. A consultant came for two days with a laptop, never touched a cow, and wrote a report. Six months later Davey was gone and the parlour was empty. I'd expect the same, only faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, oddly. Everyone thinks the tractor man is safe, but his job is half planning and ordering, sprays and seed and fuel. If the computer does that, Mr Cole might think one man can do both of our jobs. And I'm the older one.

say: I'd tell the branch the estate will **pocket the savings** from AI, not the workers.
I'd push the union for a **law to share** any money machines save.
think: Cows still need hands for now, but the land agent trusts **spreadsheets over people**.
If the estate merges two jobs into one, I'm the **older man** and likely to go.
do: Attend **every union meeting** about AI and sign the petitions that come round.
Refuse to learn **AI tools** myself and keep doing the stock work well.
Ask my son Liam to help us **put money by** each month.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then **angry**, because it repeats how the dairy herd went.
S1.quote: A consultant came for two days with a laptop, never touched a cow, and wrote a report. Six months later Davey was gone and the parlour was empty.
fieldNote: He reads Steady Disruption through the **dairy herd closure**, which he sees as decided on a screen.
He sees colleague Pete's **planning work** as more exposed than his own, and fears jobs being merged.
He plainly **refuses AI tools**; his response is collective and political, not personal retraining.

steps.text: Attend every union branch meeting that covers AI on farms
Sign and pass round the union petition on sharing machine savings
Ask son Liam to set up a monthly savings transfer
Keep the cattle records in the paper book, not the app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. And robots by 2031. I'd be 63. That's the bit I'm doing the sums on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this has to be stopped or slowed, and I'd mean it. I'd say it at the branch, at church on Fridays, to the MP's office if they'd see me. Nobody voted for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking AI in 2028 doesn't touch my hands, but it runs Mr Cole's office overnight. By 2031 there's a robot that can pull a calf and drive the quad up Long Hill. At 63 I'd lose the job and the cottage, four years before my pension. That's the whole thing, right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go to every meeting, march if there's a march, and write to the MP with Shirin's help. I'd ask Aisha if we could live with her in the city if it came to it. And I'd ask the union to fight for a rule that tied cottages can't be emptied because of robots. I wouldn't learn to run the robots. I'd rather not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'm not ashamed to say it. Maureen would be braver than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Maureen the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got three years before the robots, so let's not waste them. Then I'd go out to the cattle shed and stand there for a while. That's where I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not learn to run the robots. If the estate offered you that job, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Probably not, if I'm honest, I can't even work the phone Liam gave me. But if it was that or lose the house, Maureen would make me try. I'd hate every minute.

say: I'd say this must be **stopped or slowed**, because nobody voted for it.
I'd take that message to the **branch, church** and the MP's office.
think: Thinking AI hits the estate office first, but **robots in 2031** take my hands-on work.
At 63 I'd lose **job and cottage** four years before my pension starts.
do: Join **every march** and meeting the union calls in the first year.
Write to the **MP** with the union rep's help about tied cottages.
Ask my daughter Aisha whether we could **live with her** if we lose the house.
feel: **Frightened**, and not ashamed to say it.
Leaning on **Maureen**, who he thinks would be braver than him.
S2.quote: At 63 I'd lose the job and the cottage, four years before my pension. That's the whole thing, right there.
fieldNote: He split the dates clearly: **2028 hits the office**, 2031 hits his own job.
The **tied cottage** turns a job loss into a housing loss, which drives the alarm.
He'd **resist retraining** on robots, but admits he'd try if the house depended on it.

steps.text: Join every union march and meeting about AGI and farm jobs
Write to the MP about protecting tied-cottage tenants from robot layoffs
Ask daughter Aisha about moving in with her if the cottage goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and the robots three after that. 2034. I'd be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same at the branch: the government's got five years, so there's no excuse for not having a plan for rural workers. Houses first, then pensions. I'd say that every time someone mentions it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, 66 is close enough to my pension that I might just scrape through. But Mr Cole won't wait for the robots to arrive. Once the office AI is running in 2031, he'll plan the herd around robots coming, and he might not replace me when my knees go. It's tighter than it looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd push the union hard on the council list and housing for retired farm workers. Maureen and I would cut the car down to one and stop the Sky dish. I'd stay on the estate and keep my head down, and I'd count the months to 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a bit of hope in it. Five years is time to fight for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, money-wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, the old Corsa Maureen uses for the school run, that's £600 a year in insurance alone. She'd have to get lifts with Janet from the kitchen. Then the dish. We don't go on holiday anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Cole won't wait for the robots. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The land agent would stop buying new heifers, run the herd down quiet, and let it go when I retire. No announcement. You'd just notice the numbers going down in the shed. I've seen him do it with the pigs before the dairy.

say: I'd tell the branch the government has **five years** and no excuse for having no plan.
I'd keep saying **housing first**, then pensions, for retired farm workers.
think: At 66 I might **scrape through** to my pension before robots arrive.
The estate could quietly **run the herd down** once office AI arrives in 2031.
do: Push the union on **council housing** for retired farm workers this year.
Sell Maureen's **second car**, saving about £600 a year on insurance.
Stay on the estate and **count the months** to my pension at 67.
feel: **Anxious**, with some **hope** that five years leaves time to fight.
S3.quote: The land agent would stop buying new heifers, run the herd down quiet, and let it go when I retire. No announcement.
fieldNote: He spots that the estate can **plan around robots** years before they arrive.
Five years lets him **hope to scrape** to his pension, which softens his mood from the two-year case.
Practical cuts are small and specific: the **second car** and the TV dish.

steps.text: Press the union to campaign for council homes for retired farm workers
Sell the old Corsa and share lifts to the school kitchen
Stay on the estate herd until the state pension at 67

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2039 for the robots. I'd be 71 and long gone from the estate. Even so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so let's see the government do it right. I'd want the union in the room when they write the rules. That's my public line and I'd stick to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the robots aren't my problem in this one, I'll have retired. My problem is still the cottage. I retire at 67, I hand back the keys, and Maureen and I have nowhere and nothing saved. That's true whether the robot comes or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on the union's housing campaign properly, not just signing things. I'd sit down with Aisha and Liam this Christmas and talk about where we'd live. And I'd keep working the herd as long as my knees let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not panicky. Worried, a slow kind of worry. More for Liam, really, because lorries go to robots too, don't they?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Liam about his own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Liam to learn something a robot can't do before he's my age, because I never did. He'd laugh at me. He thinks I'm a dinosaur, and maybe I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this ten-year picture that you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the robots on the night shifts in lambing, if I'm honest. Nobody wants to be out in the sleet at two in the morning at seventy. But I'd want it to be a man who gets the money from that, not a company.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** to get the rules right.
I'd want the **union in the room** when the government writes those rules.
think: Robots come after I retire, so the **cottage** is still my real problem.
I hand back the keys at 67 with **nothing saved**, robots or not.
do: Join the union's **housing campaign** properly, not just sign petitions.
Talk to Aisha and Liam this **Christmas** about where we'd live.
Keep working the **herd** as long as my knees allow.
feel: More **worried for his son**, whose lorry driving could go to robots too.
S4.quote: I'd tell my son Liam to learn something a robot can't do before he's my age, because I never did.
fieldNote: With ten years, the robots fall **after his retirement**, but his mood stays tied to the cottage.
His worry shifts toward his **son's job**, a sign he feels personally clear of the machines.
He grudgingly sees value in robots for **night lambing**, if workers share the gain.

steps.text: Volunteer on the union housing campaign for retired farm workers
Talk with Aisha and Liam at Christmas about where to live
Keep working the suckler herd until the knees give out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Robots by the time I'm 63, and the house goes with the job. What would help is a law that says a man who's worked a tied cottage twenty years can't be put out at the end, and council homes that actually get built in villages like ours.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the house, really, and the house is everything. People think farming is about the land. For the likes of me it's about who owns the roof. I've worked this estate twenty-three years and I don't own a brick of it.

headlineQuote: I've worked this estate twenty-three years and I don't own a brick of it.
portrait: Yusuf is a 58-year-old **livestock man** on a large estate, living in a **tied cottage** that goes with the job.
He has about **three weeks of savings**, low pay and few other farm jobs within twenty miles.
He never uses **AI tools** and turns to the **union** and politics rather than retraining.
His mood follows the **robot date** against his pension at 67, but the cottage worries him in every picture.
He blames **distant decision-makers**, from the land agent's consultant to whoever profits from machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots in 2031 would take his job and **home** at 63.
whatWouldHelp: A **law protecting** long-serving tied-cottage tenants from eviction at the end of their work.
**Council homes** actually built in villages like his.
